notes.meaning: Paul and Barnabas arrived in Iconium and went straight to the Jewish meeting place, the synagogue. They shared the good news about Jesus with such clarity and spiritual power that many Jews and Greeks believed. Even after facing hard times in the last city, they did not hold back from sharing the truth. God often uses simple, bold words to draw people to Himself.

Some of the Jewish leaders refused to believe the message about Jesus. They stirred up the Gentiles, who were non-Jewish people, and turned their minds against the believers. These opponents spread harmful lies to create bitter feelings toward the new Christians.

Instead of running away from the angry talk, the missionaries stayed in Iconium for a long time. They spoke fearlessly, relying on the Lord and His free favor toward sinners, which is called grace. The Lord proved their words were true by giving them power to perform amazing miracles.

differ.view: Miraculous signs were temporary gifts given to confirm the apostles' message before the New Testament was finished, and they faded away afterward.
God still confirms the preaching of the gospel today with the same kinds of signs and wonders.

notes.meaning: The message forced the people in the city to take sides. Some citizens agreed with the Jewish leaders who rejected the gospel, while others stood with Paul and Barnabas. This is the first place in the book of Acts where Barnabas and Paul are called apostles, meaning messengers sent out with Christ's authority.

The opponents formed an angry mob of both Jews and Gentiles, supported by their local leaders. They hatched a violent plot to mistreat the apostles and stone them to death. Stoning was a brutal way to kill someone by hurling heavy rocks at them.

Paul and Barnabas learned about the secret plot and escaped safely. They traveled to the nearby towns of Lystra and Derbe, as well as the surrounding countryside. Even though they had to flee for their lives, they never stopped preaching the good news.

In Lystra, a man was sitting by the road who had never been able to walk. His feet had been completely paralyzed from the day he was born. Luke mentions these facts to make it clear that human medicine could never cure him.

The lame man sat listening intently as Paul preached the message of Jesus. Paul looked directly into his eyes and sensed that the man trusted God's power to make him well. Faith was growing in the man's heart as he heard the word of God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some faith healers teach that sick people are always healed if they have enough faith, so a lack of healing means the sick person failed to believe.

notes.meaning: Paul spoke out in a loud voice so that everyone around could hear, commanding the man to stand up. Instantly, the man jumped straight to his feet and began walking all around. His sudden leap proved that his cure was complete and came only from God.

When the local crowd saw the lame man walking, they shouted with excitement in their native Lycaonian tongue. They thought that their pagan gods had taken human form and come down to visit them. Because they used their own dialect, the apostles did not realize at first what the people were saying.

The crowd named Barnabas Zeus, the chief Greek god, perhaps because he carried himself with quiet dignity. They called Paul Hermes, the messenger god, because he was the main speaker. An old local myth said these two gods had once visited that very region in disguise.

The priest of Zeus served at a temple located just outside the city entrance. He brought bulls decorated with floral wreaths to the gates so that he and the crowds could offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas. They wanted to honor the two men as if they were heavenly beings.

As soon as Barnabas and Paul understood what was happening, they tore their clothes in deep shock and grief. Tearing one's clothing was an ancient Jewish sign of horror at blasphemy, which means showing disrespect to God. They rushed straight into the middle of the crowd to stop the sacrifice.

The apostles cried out that they were ordinary, frail human beings just like everyone else. They explained that their goal was to lead the people away from empty idols to the one true, living God. This real God is the Creator who made the sky, the land, the sea, and everything in them.

Paul told them that in past ages, God permitted the Gentile nations to live without His written laws. He let them follow their own foolish ideas and false religions. Yet this long history of pagan worship did not make their idols real or right.

Even without a written Bible, God showed His kindness to all people every day. He sent rain from heaven to water the earth and gave regular harvest seasons so people would have plenty to eat. These daily gifts in nature were living proof of God's goodness and constant care.

Even after Paul gave this clear speech about the Creator, the crowd was determined to offer sacrifices. The apostles had to work very hard to keep the excited people from treating them like gods. Human hearts easily latch onto false religion instead of the true God.

Enemies traveled over a hundred miles from Antioch and Iconium just to cause trouble. They poisoned the minds of the crowds and convinced them to turn against Paul. The mob hurled stones at Paul until they thought he was dead, then dragged his battered body outside the city walls.

A small group of believers gathered around Paul's body, likely weeping and praying for him. Remarkably, Paul stood right back up and walked into the city with them. The very next day, he felt well enough to travel on to Derbe with Barnabas.

In Derbe, Paul and Barnabas preached the good news and guided many people into becoming followers of Jesus. Afterward, they bravely turned around and revisited Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch. They willingly risked their lives to care for the infant churches in places where they had just been attacked.

The apostles spent time building up the young believers, urging them to hold tight to their faith in Christ. They warned them that every Christian must pass through many painful trials before entering the kingdom of God. Hardships are not a sign of God's failure, but part of the road believers walk.

differ.view: Continuing in the faith through hardship proves that a believer's faith is real, because God preserves His chosen people to the end.

notes.meaning: Paul and Barnabas set apart trusted leaders, called elders, to guide each local flock. They prayed and fasted together to ask for God's wisdom, then placed the leaders and congregations into the Lord's hands. Good spiritual leadership helps protect and feed the church.

differ.view: The congregations selected their own elders by a show of hands in a vote, with the apostles overseeing the process.
The apostles chose and ordained the elders with the consent of the people, acting with pastoral oversight like bishops.
Pastors were appointed with the election and approval of the congregation so that preaching would continue regularly in every church.

notes.meaning: The two missionaries traveled back through the region of Pisidia until they reached Pamphylia on the southern coast. They preached the message of the Lord in the city of Perga, which they had passed through earlier. Then they went down to Attalia, a busy seaport, to catch a ship.

From Attalia, they sailed across the sea back to Antioch in Syria. This was the home church that had originally placed them in God's caring hands when their missionary trip began. They returned home knowing they had finished the work God gave them to do.

When they reached home, they called a meeting of the whole church family. They shared wonderful stories of how God had protected them and worked through their preaching. Best of all, they explained how God had opened the door of faith so non-Jewish people could be saved.

Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch for a long time, resting and encouraging the disciples there. Their first missionary journey had succeeded completely under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Christian fellowship gave them joy and strength after enduring so many hardships.
